phrase: You buy bitcoin at the price you deserve
note: A popular Bitcoin saying: the price you pay mirrors how early you understood it. Buying late, or selling early, is the tuition of learning slowly.

phrase: For the tuition you earned
note: 'Paying tuition' is trader slang for losing money while learning how markets work. The lesson is expensive but, ideally, you only pay it once.

phrase: We saw the dot com bubble that bursted
note: In the late 1990s investors piled into internet start-ups. When that bubble burst from 2000, the tech-heavy Nasdaq lost nearly 80% and many companies vanished.

phrase: And that’s a zero sum game
note: In a zero-sum game one player's gain is exactly another's loss. Chasing paper profits can work that way: digits change hands and nothing new is created.

phrase: It’s too big to fail
note: 'Too big to fail' names banks so large that governments rescue them rather than let them collapse, as in the 2008 bailouts. Bitcoin's first block quotes a headline about a bank bailout.

phrase:
Might sell with sell pressure
But no liquidity
note: Sell pressure is a wave of people trying to exit. Liquidity is how easily you can sell without crashing the price. When liquidity dries up, sellers find no buyers at a fair price.

phrase: Are straight up owners of debt
note: In a debt-based system, lenders and bondholders get paid first. When firms fail, creditors sit ahead of shareholders, and cash savers quietly lose to inflation.

phrase: Commercial lien that’s a fatal error
note: A lien is a legal claim over someone's property until a debt is paid. Miss the payments and the lender can seize the asset: you own it only until you don't.

phrase: Hate the game and still have to be a player
note: A twist on 'don't hate the player, hate the game'. You can dislike the fiat money system and still live inside it, so learn its rules and play them better.

phrase: Money don’t grow on trees
note: The history of money, from metal to paper to digital, runs through the Saylor Series: 17 long conversations between Michael Saylor and Robert Breedlove on the What is Money? podcast.

phrase: Before that, pressed out of metal
note: Hard money started as metal. Gold, silver and copper coins carried value for thousands of years. The earliest known coins were struck in Lydia, in what is now Turkey, more than 2,500 years ago.

phrase: Pressed ink on paper sheets
note: Metal is heavy to carry, so banks issued paper notes as claims on the coins and gold in their vaults. Paper became a stand-in for the real thing.

phrase: Promissory notes were great receipts
note: A promissory note is a written promise to pay. Early banknotes were exactly that: receipts redeemable for gold or silver on demand, until governments cut the link.

phrase: Until the bank run made them see
note: A bank run is when many depositors withdraw at once, fearing the bank cannot pay. Banks lend out most deposits, so they never hold enough cash to repay everyone at the same time.

phrase: Restricted access, leaky faucet
note: Money held by someone else can be frozen or capped: restricted access. Inflation is the leaky faucet, value dripping out of savings so slowly most people never notice.

phrase: Insurance don’t cover pyramid below
note: A pyramid scheme pays early members with money from later ones and collapses when new money stops. Critics say debt-based money has a similar shape, with the most exposed at the bottom.

phrase: From penthouse down when the hotel floods
note: New money enters at the top, through banks and asset owners, before it reaches everyone else. Economists call that the Cantillon effect: first in line gain while the floors below take the hit.

phrase: Don’t wanna let that sink in
note: In October 2022 Elon Musk walked into Twitter's San Francisco headquarters carrying a bathroom sink, posting 'let that sink in!' days before closing his US$44 billion purchase of the company, now X.

phrase: Quick realize paddler missing
note: A twist on 'up the creek without a paddle': stuck in trouble with no way to steer. Lose your savings in a crisis and you are adrift.

phrase: They did me like how they reboot yeezy
note: A nod to an internet conspiracy meme claiming Kanye West (Ye) was secretly replaced by a clone or body double. There is no evidence for it.

phrase:
Where’s my money?
It’s in the vault
note: A bank vault holds only a fraction of what depositors are owed. Most of 'your' money is a number on the bank's books, already lent out to someone else.

phrase:
Can I get it out now?
Maybe tomorrow
note: In Australia, getting cash out of a bank is not always instant. Large withdrawals can need notice, ATMs cap how much you take per day, and staff may quiz you on why you want your own money, citing scam and money-laundering rules.

phrase: You know it’s my money
note: Self-custody is the Bitcoin reply: you hold the keys, so no teller, branch or bank policy gets to say 'maybe tomorrow'. Be your own bank.
